newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria opposition urges Commonwealth on detainees.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria opposition urges Commonwealth on detainees.

text.p: Nigeria's opposition on Monday appealed to Commonwealth ministers to press for the release of political detainees during talks with the military government on restoring democracy.

The Commonwealth team left London for Nigeria's capital Abuja without a key member of the group, Canadian Secretary of State for Latin America and Africa Christine Stewart who dropped out after Nigeria declined to issue visas to two Canadian security officers due to accompany the delegation.
The ministers are expected to hold talks with officials on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"We plead that (military ruler) General Sani Abacha should be prevailed upon, and if necessary compelled by appropriate means...to release within a stipulated time Moshood Abiola and all other detainees," the umbrella NADECO opposition group said in an open memorandum to the Commonwealth ministers.

The ministers are, however, unlikely to meet Abacha. Neither will they see opposition groups like NADECO that are campaigning for power to be handed over to Abiola, a wealthy businessman presumed to have won an annulled 1993 presidential election.

Abiola has been detained since 1994 when he defied the military government and proclaimed himself president on the basis of the 1993 vote. The 1993 annulment plunged Africa's most populous nation into political turmoil.
Many of his supporters are also detained or have fled into exile in Britain and the United States.

The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria last year after it hanged nine minority rights activists, including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, but since then splits have emerged on how best to push Abuja back to democracy.

The eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) resolved its differences in September when it decided not to impose a set of agreed sanctions on Nigeria and instead to keep the dialogue going by sending a fact-finding mission.
Nigeria refused to allow a fact-finding mission, saying the United Nations had undertaken a similar assignment.
"The meeting in Abuja tomorrow and on Wednesday is strictly a continuation of the talks we held with the Commonwealth in London," said a senior foreign ministry official.
The two sides first met in May in London where Nigeria insisted that its suspension was unfair and until this was lifted there would be no progress on any other issue.
The absence at the Abuja talks of Canada, which favours a hard line against the Nigerian government, will be blow to local opposition groups.
"The Canadians are the only ones serious about a showdown with the junta in Abuja," said a NADECO spokesman.
In the memorandum signed by its leader Michael Ajasin and distributed to embassies, NADECO berated Britain, accusing it of soft-pedaling on Nigeria.
"The British government surprisingly seems to have intensified its lobby of other Commonwealth countries to soft-pedal on the Auckland Commonwealth sanctions against the Abacha junta."
The 53-nation Commonwealth, which mainly groups Britain and its former colonies, wants Abacha to restore democracy before his set date of October 1, 1998.
CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia.
